title: Dungeness
author: Lexi Zotomayor
excerpt: After months cooped up in an apartment, even a ferry ride felt like a reprieve. Hiking Cumberland Island's unpaved roads—kept intact by the National Park Service—took me past Dungeness, Stafford, and Plum Orchard, and left me wondering why the Carnegies walked away from northern high society.
bodyText:
Had I possessed unlimited means, I would have given in to my wanderlust with complete abandon. Life, of course, held other plans. It tantalized me, letting me loose on occasion, though always on a short leash.

Visiting an island off the coast of Georgia years ago felt like a sudden reprieve after months of being cooped up in an apartment. By then, I welcomed any excuse to leave the house, even if it meant nothing more ambitious than a run to the supermarket or the corner gas station.

Cumberland Island can be reached only by ferry, which meant leaving the car behind on the mainland.

At the outset, the excursion promised nothing but disappointment. I stepped off the boat with a heavy heart, dragging my feet through loose sand and braving air thick with humidity.

Ten minutes into our walk, the path opened onto the skeleton of a great house. They called it Dungeness. Only the brick-and-stone outer walls and a cluster of tall chimneys remained standing, open to the sky. Live oaks draped in Spanish moss leaned in toward the empty window frames, and palmettos pushed up through the grass where parlor floors had once been. For a moment, the heat and the heavy walk fell away. The place had belonged to the Carnegies—the same steel-and-philanthropy family whose name sits above the entrance to Carnegie Hall in New York.

![Top/aerial view of Dungeness](/assets/uploads/cms/dungeness03.jpg "Top view of the estate/NPS PHOTO")

Here, as in hundreds of parks across this vast nation, the National Park Service has kept its hand steady and light—preserving the ground without paving it over or turning it into a theme park. Without shuttle buses or asphalt roads, simply getting from Dungeness up toward Stafford Plantation and Plum Orchard turned into a brisk, unplanned march. Along the way, the Carnegies' hold on the island came into focus: Stafford with its old tabby slave cabins and broad fields, and Plum Orchard farther north, a grand Georgian Revival mansion built for Thomas Carnegie’s son George—still standing, unlike its burned-out neighbor to the south.

![Carnegie Family](/assets/uploads/cms/lucycolemancarnegiefamily.jpg "The Carnegie Family at the steps of their Dungeness home.")

Farther down the trail, we ducked into a small museum. Placards on the wall explained that a fire had gutted Dungeness in 1959, and that long before the Carnegies arrived, the island had served as a contested military outpost. A sixteenth-century Spanish cabasset sat inside a glass case, offering proof.

The island holds four thousand years of human history, beginning with the Timucua people. Spanish friars and soldiers arrived with their missions, followed by the British, and later by a plantation era that lasted until Revolutionary War General Nathanael Greene claimed the land and built the original Dungeness. A full century passed before the Carnegies arrived to raise their own estates on the foundations.

Watching *The Gilded Age* years later sent my mind straight back to those scorched walls. Having read more about the period since my visit, I can look back at the ruins with sharper eyes.

Still, one question lingers. Why did Thomas Carnegie and his family decamp to Georgia’s largest barrier island, so far removed from Pittsburgh, Manhattan, and Newport? While Mrs. Astor’s Four Hundred and Alva Vanderbilt’s thousand-guest galas were busy rubbing elbows in northern drawing rooms, the Carnegies packed their trunks for a sandbar off Georgia.
